archetype.name: Pocket Passer (precision)
archetype.definition: An accuracy-first distributor who wins from the shotgun with timing and ball placement into the 10-to-19-yard window. He doesn't use his legs or force tight windows.

report.headline: Accuracy at a career-best clip, with a scheme built to keep him throwing
report.take:
Burrow has always been at his best as an accuracy passer. He led the league in CPOE in 2021 and ranked third in 2024. This season he has gone past both of those years. He is completing 74.2% of his passes with a 9.44 CPOE (2nd of 55), and he leads all qualifiers in passing yards per game (309.5), touchdowns per game (2.9) and passing EPA per game (10.1). He has started every week and practiced fully heading into the stretch run. This is a healthy version of the player Cincinnati built around, and right now he is outperforming his own best seasons.

The production comes from the intermediate middle of the field. His 82 throws of 10 to 19 air yards have added 63.1 EPA at 0.769 a play with an 18.1 CPOE. His 204 short attempts have added 30.7 between them. Everything thrown 10+ yards has produced 102.6 EPA, and everything under 10 has produced 18.2. Tee Higgins (0.70 EPA per target) and Mike Gesicki (0.648) have been the most efficient way to move this offense, with Ja'Marr Chase taking the most targets. The structure also pushes volume his way. Cincinnati passes 13 points more often than situation predicts, the most in the league. The run game ranks 19th in EPA, and a defense that is 31st against the run keeps games close and high-scoring. He has also cut his pressure-to-sack rate to 19.5%, well below the roughly 30% marks of past seasons. That is a big reason his sack rate sits at 4.8% against a league average of 7.8%.

There are a few caveats under the headline numbers. His aggressiveness (tight-window throws) has fallen to 12.89% from 17.4% last year. He isn't threading needles more often. His receivers are open more, and he's hitting them. His bad-throw rate has climbed to 8.9% from last year's 5.0%, but 2025 was the outlier. He sat between 10% and 14% in every earlier season, so this is his normal level rather than decline. The parts most likely to cool are the hot pockets on small samples: 21 red-zone touchdowns on 57 attempts with a 17.6 CPOE, and a 1.198 EPA per deep attempt on only 33 throws. Turnovers are the one real blemish. His six interceptions rank 37th of 55, three came in a single shootout with Tennessee, and five of the six went to the right side.

He is getting better as the season goes on. Over his last five games he is at 0.362 EPA per dropback with 18 touchdowns and a 13.5 CPOE. That run includes four straight games of 14+ passing EPA from Week 7 to Week 10. The Week 11 loss at Washington was his flattest game since September, with a 2.6 CPOE and 8.2 EPA, and it came with starting guard Dalton Risner and receiver Andrei Iosivas inactive. Expect the efficiency to settle somewhere between this pace and his 2024 level. The volume is built into the offense and should keep him near the top of the position.

strengths.title: Owns the intermediate window
strengths.body: His 10-to-19-yard throws are the most productive part of any QB profile in this dossier, at 0.769 EPA a play with an 18.1 CPOE. Those throws come from timing and placement on in-breakers and outs, not from tight-window gambles. The skill itself is durable because he has been a top-tier accuracy passer for years. The exact rate will drift down from this level.

strengths.title: Pressure no longer becomes sacks
strengths.body: He is pressured at a middling rate (20.7%, 20th of 45), but only 19.5% of those pressures end in sacks, which ranks 7th. In earlier seasons that figure sat around 30% or higher. A 2.71-second time to throw and the quick game are helping him beat pressure. This is the biggest change from his past profile and the one most worth watching. Some regression toward his career norm is plausible.

strengths.title: A pass-first offense with three targets
strengths.body: Cincinnati leans on the pass harder than any offense in the league relative to situation. Higgins, Chase and Gesicki all post strong per-target EPA, so defenses can't load up on one read. With a bottom-tier run defense forcing points, the volume is structural and should last.

concerns.title: Efficiency above his own ceiling
concerns.body: A 9.44 CPOE beats his best previous seasons (6.64 in 2021, 6.787 in 2024). His red-zone line of 21 TDs on 57 attempts with a 17.6 CPOE is very hot. He is a top accuracy passer, but these numbers run ahead of even his history. Expect the touchdown rate and CPOE to settle lower rather than collapse.

concerns.title: Interceptions come in clusters
concerns.body: Six interceptions rank only 37th of 55. Three came in the Week 8 shootout with Tennessee, and five of the six went to the right side. Two came in just 21 no-huddle snaps. He tends to force the ball when games turn frantic, which fits his long-running pattern of double-digit-interception full seasons. It is a real, modest flaw rather than a trend getting worse.

concerns.title: Dead plays behind the line
concerns.body: His 59 throws behind the line of scrimmage have cost 12.5 EPA. Chase Brown's 62 targets are running at -0.149 EPA each. Together with a 19th-ranked run game and weak under-center results, the non-passing parts of the offense drag. That is a role and scheme cost more than a flaw in Burrow, but it limits how efficient the full offense can be.

trend.note: The first month was uneven: negative EPA in the opener and five sacks at Houston. From Week 7 to Week 10 he strung together four straight games of 14+ passing EPA. The Week 11 dip at Washington came with a starting guard out and stops short of breaking the trend.

nextGame.headline: The league's leakiest deep defense meets his best-throwing stretch
nextGame.body:
New Orleans fits his profile almost perfectly. The Saints rank 20th in pass EPA allowed and 25th in explosive pass rate. They rank dead last in deep EPA allowed at 0.962, the one area where his small-sample numbers are already extreme. They have also been soft on lead receivers: WR1s score 3.3 PPR points over their averages against them (28th) at 0.39 EPA a target. Their tight-end defense is 28th by EPA. The one real counter is the pass rush, which ranks 7th in sack rate. That matters for an offensive line that just played without a starter.

Availability tilts things further toward Cincinnati. The Saints are without CB Martin Emerson Jr. (46% of snaps), LB Pete Werner (74%) and DT Christen Miller, which thins the coverage behind that rush. Their offense is also missing two starting tackles and center Erik McCoy, which makes a long shootout less likely. On his side, guard Dalton Risner (94% of snaps) was inactive last week and carries an estimated return of this game; his status is the key protection variable. Iosivas's thumb surgery costs only a rotational receiver. The Book has Cincinnati -10 with a 50.5 total. That points to a comfortable lead, which is the one game state where his EPA dips (0.164 when up nine or more).

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots against a broken secondary
keyMatchups.body: He is averaging 1.198 EPA on 20+ yard throws against a defense that ranks last in deep EPA allowed. With Emerson out, the Saints have even less depth to cover downfield. If Cincinnati takes early shots, this is where a big passing day would come from.

keyMatchups.title: Chase against a soft WR1 defense
keyMatchups.body: Chase has 96 targets and gets 0.473 EPA each. New Orleans ranks 28th at limiting opposing WR1s. Burrow's target tree is concentrated enough that a soft spot for the top receiver turns into his passing yardage directly.

keyMatchups.title: Saints rush versus a patched line
keyMatchups.body: The Saints' one defensive strength is getting home, with a 7th-ranked sack rate. Burrow's low pressure-to-sack rate has neutralized rushes all year. If Risner can't go, the interior is where that skill gets tested hardest.

nextGame.watch: Whether Cincinnati keeps attacking downfield after building a two-score lead, or turns into a run-the-clock offense in the second half.

restOfSeason.body:
The volume is real: the most pass-heavy offense relative to situation, three efficient targets, and a defense that rarely lets him coast. That supports something close to his 309.5 yards a game. The touchdown pace will not hold. A 17-game pace of 49 passing TDs depends on red-zone and deep-ball rates that are hot on small samples, and his CPOE is above his career best. I'd project 275 to 325 passing yards and 2.1 to 2.8 touchdowns a game. That still puts him in the top tier of the position, with efficiency closer to his 2024 season than to his last five games.

Interceptions should run 0.4 to 0.8 a game, arriving in bunches in shootouts rather than steadily. The pressure-to-sack improvement is the change most likely to give back some ground, since it runs well ahead of every prior season. His floor is protected by the volume and his accuracy. The biggest risk to his ceiling is game script: in comfortable leads the offense gets more conservative and his EPA dips.
swingFactors: Offensive line health, starting with Risner at guard
Red-zone TD rate cooling from its current level
Whether the run defense keeps forcing shootouts

confidence.note: Ten full starts, a stable role and supporting cast, and accuracy traits backed by years of history; only the touchdown and CPOE rates are likely to come down.
